title: Settings in an analytics tool
excerpt: Keep the pinned metric, its definition, the window, and the source status on the first settings screen. Rare controls stay lower, and definition changes say whether history will be restated.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it, a single place to change what the number means.
caption: The rule sits on the machine that serves the number. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which analytics settings belong on the first screen?
faqs.answer: The pinned metric, the published definition, the default window and comparison, the account time zone, source freshness, and who receives the Monday note. Personal pins should be labeled as personal, so they are not confused with the company number. Theme and warehouse trivia can wait.

faqs.question: What should happen when a definition changes?
faqs.answer: Keep a draft off the homepage until an owner publishes it. Before a change restates past days, say so, and mark those points as updated. The sentence under the number and the sentence in settings should be the same field, not two copies that drift.

faqs.question: How should a disconnected source appear?
faqs.answer: On the source row, in words, with the time it failed, and on the number that depends on it. Say whether this role can reconnect. Disconnecting should explain what the home number will do next, warning or hiding, and only offer behaviors you have actually built.

markdown:
Keep analytics tool settings ux as a cabinet, not a second product. Group what the operator who needs one trusted number changes often, and bury the rest where it cannot rewrite Monday by accident.

The W3C's WCAG overview holds interfaces to four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A setting passes when the label says what will change for the number, the control can be operated without a guessing game, and the same concept keeps the same name on the chart and in the cabinet.

## The frequent shelf

Put on the first settings screen only the decisions that change the figure people cite.

- Which metric is pinned for this role, and the sentence that defines it.
- The default window, and what it is compared with.
- The account time zone and the week start, because both change "last 7 days."
- Which sources are connected, and which one is stale.
- Who receives the scheduled Monday note.

Theme, avatar, API playgrounds, and the warehouse dialect can wait on a lower shelf. They are real. They are not why someone opened settings after a number looked wrong. A cabinet that leads with appearance has mixed up a costume with the instrument.

Labels should be outcomes. "Window used on the home number," not "Default temporal configuration." "Definition readers see under paid invoices," not "Semantic layer." The operator is busy and already unsure. A label that needs a glossary is a label that will be mis-set.

Separate personal preferences from company definitions. One person's pinned metric is not the company's definition of revenue. Put personal choices in a group called "For you." Put definitions in a group called "For everyone," and say who may edit them. Mixing the two is how a private experiment becomes the number in the board pack.

## Definitions live here, and on the chart

The definition sentence is a setting with a public face. Edit it in the cabinet, and show the same words under the number. If those two can drift, they will, and trust goes with them. One field, two renderings. Not a wiki page nobody links.

Publish and draft should be different states. An analyst can draft "count a workspace as active after the second invite." The homepage should keep the published sentence until an owner publishes the draft. Say that on the draft. "Not on the home number yet." A save button that rewrites history without a publish step is too much power for a Tuesday afternoon.

When a definition change would restate past days, say so before it saves. "This will change the last 90 days. The points will be marked as updated." Offer to apply it from today forward if that is what they meant. Silent restatement is an error even when the new math is better. The cabinet's job is to make the consequence visible.

Rounding, tax, and refunds belong in the definition, not in a buried advanced toggle. If paid invoices exclude tax, the sentence says so. Do not make someone open three accordions to learn why finance's spreadsheet is different. If you need an advanced control, it still needs a plain label and a line about who is affected.

## Sources, freshness, and the dangerous switch

The source group should list each connection in human words. "Billing, healthy, refreshed 20 minutes ago." "Product database, disconnected since 4:10 am." The fix sits on the row if this role can reconnect, and a sentence sits there if they cannot. "An owner has to reconnect this." A single "integrations" page of logos, with no freshness, is not a setting. It is a poster.

Disconnecting a source is dangerous. Say what the home number will do without it. "Paid invoices will show the last good total and wear a warning," or "Paid invoices will be hidden because they would be incomplete." Let them choose only among true behaviors. Do not offer a toggle you have not built.

Time zone changes are almost as dangerous. Moving the account from UTC to a local zone will move every day boundary. Say that upcoming days will use the new zone, and that past days stay as they were stored, or that you will restate them. Pick one, write it, and show a preview of "today" before and after. A dropdown of cities with no preview will be set wrong and discovered in a meeting.

Scheduled sends are settings, not a campaign tool. One Monday note, who it goes to, which pinned number it includes, and whether it sends when the number is stale. Default to not sending a stale figure, or to sending it with the stale sentence in the first line. A cheerful email of a blank or a zero is worse than silence. Show the last note that went out, so the owner can see the voice and the digits together.

## Who may touch the cabinet

Permissions for settings should be visible in the cabinet itself. If a regional lead can change their own pin and cannot change the company definition, the definition field should say so while they are looking at it, not after they type for ten minutes and fail to save. Disabled, with the reason beside it, beats hidden for anything they would reasonably seek. Hidden is fine for the billing card they have no cause to expect.

Inviting a teammate is a setting with a role attached. Ask for the role in the same step as the email, in the same nouns the rest of the product uses. Do not invite them as "admin" and sort it out later. Later is how margin leaks into a guest seat.

Tokens and embeds are easy to forget because they are not people. List them beside the seats. "Board embed, home number only, no drill-down, created in January." Revoke sits on the row. An embed is a permission that lives on someone else's site. It deserves a plainer label than a client secret pasted into a developer page.

Audit the dangerous saves. "Definition of paid invoices published by Riley, Tuesday." Keep that line on the definition, not only in a log. The person questioning the number should see when the meaning moved. A log they cannot find will not settle the question.

## Pins, targets, and the note beside the number

A target is a setting, because it changes what "good" means on the first screen. If paid invoices have a monthly target, show the target's owner and the period in the cabinet, and show the same words next to the comparison on the home number. A target with no owner will be doubted the week it is missed. A target that lives only in a slide will be quoted anyway, and then the product looks wrong for being right.

The note that explains an ugly day, "tracking was down on the 4th," is also a setting in the loose sense: it is a sentence the company has agreed to attach to a figure. Keep it short, dated, and visible to everyone who can see the figure. Do not make it a comment thread. The first screen has room for one caveat, not a discussion. If the discussion is still open, the note should say the figure is under review, which is a stronger status than a quiet asterisk.

Personal pins should be easy to change and hard to confuse with the company default. "You pinned failed payments. The company home is still paid invoices." Two sentences, in the cabinet and on the screen the first time they pin. After that, the screen they use is theirs, and a link returns to the company number. Forcing one homepage on every role makes the tool feel like a poster. Letting every pin rewrite the poster makes it feel like a rumor.

## Review it against Monday

Change the pin, and confirm the home screen agrees, including the copy-to-clipboard line. Change the definition as a draft, and confirm Monday still shows the published sentence. Disconnect a test source, and confirm the number warns instead of zeroing. Move the time zone in a sandbox, and read the preview of today out loud.

If any frequent change took more than a minute to find, it is on the wrong shelf. If any rare change was sitting at the top, move it down. The cabinet is finished when a skeptical operator can predict what the home number will do after a save.

The next product in this series is no longer a chart. It is a queue. [The first screen of a support inbox](/blog/the-first-screen-of-a-support-inbox) asks a different question: what is the next conversation, and what is the one action. The same discipline applies. Name the object. Do not open with a tour.

Hanabi designs settings in Figma next to the screen they affect, then builds them in Next.js, React, and TypeScript so the preview and the live number share a definition. Tailwind keeps the cabinet visually quiet. PostgreSQL and Prisma are a fit for the published sentence, the source status, and the pin, which are data, not decorations.

If your settings have become a catalog of toggles and the home number still surprises people, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the figure you need operators to trust, and the three settings that change it. The call should decide what sits on the frequent shelf.
